items.title: NCSC-2026-0448 [1.00] [H/H] Kwetsbaarheden verholpen in Oracle Fusion Middleware
items.excerpt: Oracle heeft meerdere kwetsbaarheden verholpen in diverse producten, waaronder Oracle SOA Suite, Oracle WebLogic Server, Oracle Data Integrator, Oracle Identity Manager, Oracle Access Manager, Oracle WebCenter Content, Oracle Fusion Middleware (inclusief Helidon) en Oracle HTTP Server. De kwetsbaarheden betreffen onder andere onveilige deserialisatie, onvoldoende authenticatie- en toegangscontroles, kwetsbaarheden in netwerkprotocollen zoals HTTP, HTTP/2, SOAP, T3, IIOP en LDAP, en fouten in cryptografische bibliotheken zoals Bouncy Castle en Jackson-databind. Aanvallers kunnen hierdoor onder meer: - Arbitrary code execution uitvoeren via crafted input of deserialisatieprocessen. - Volledige systeemcompromittering bereiken via netwerktoegang zonder authenticatie. - Ongeautoriseerde toegang verkrijgen tot gevoelige of kritieke data. - Data manipuleren, creëren, verwijderen of wijzigen zonder juiste rechten. - Denial-of-Service veroorzaken door resource-uitputting, crashes of hangs. - Privilege escalation uitvoeren binnen het systeem. - Cross-site scripting en spoofing aanvallen uitvoeren. - Kwetsbaarheden in authenticatie- en autorisatiemechanismen misbruiken. items.title: Camera Management Software Compromise Leads to Malware Deployment
items.excerpt: Attackers compromised camera management software to deploy malware, establish persistence, and beacon to C2. Huntress breaks down the attack chain and IOCs.

items.title: It was a matter of when, not if...
items.excerpt: Security people always say it’s not a matter of if, but when you get hacked. It took us (almost) seven years but we can now say that we’re the hackers that got hacked. We noticed suspicious activity, investigated, and came to the inevitable conclusion that damn, we got hacked. So what do hackers do when they get hacked? Handle it the way we think it should be handled. That is open, transparent and honest, even if it sucks. So far, we’ve been in full incident response mode, blocked access to our infrastructure and started a forensics investigation with the assistance of a third party incident response team.

items.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
items.excerpt: The September Microsoft Patch Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like?
